title: The problem and the promised outcome
teaching: Start by separating the pain we experienced from the product outcome we are committing to deliver.
question: What specific delivery failures is Mission Rail fixing, and what observable outcome would prove the replacement works?
whyItMatters: If the problem and outcome are vague, the new system can reproduce the old complexity with cleaner names.

title: The rules that constrain every design
teaching: These principles decide which safety guarantees remain and which forms of ceremony must disappear.
question: Which principles are non-negotiable, and where would you push back if implementation made the rail slower or more complicated?
whyItMatters: The principles are the test for future design decisions that the architecture cannot predict today.

title: Identity and the pure mission rail
teaching: Canonical identity answers what exact thing is being discussed; the pure rail answers the one legal next action without performing effects.
question: Why must canonical identity and next-action calculation be separate, pure package responsibilities?
whyItMatters: This boundary prevents filesystem, model, or host behavior from changing the meaning of mission state.

title: Guided Review as the human steering surface
teaching: Guided Review lets the human understand, challenge, and steer plans, exact code, and QA without reading agent transcripts.
question: At which moments should Guided Review appear, and what information must it provide for you to make a meaningful decision?
whyItMatters: This is how autonomy remains understandable instead of turning the human into either a bottleneck or a spectator.

title: Deterministic history and reusable lanes
teaching: The store owns replayable history while lane lifecycle owns assignment, reconciliation, and return-to-ready decisions.
question: How do deterministic replay and stable Alpha, Bravo, and Charlie lanes prevent completed work from becoming stranded or ambiguous?
whyItMatters: Durable state and reusable workspaces address two of the most expensive failures in the original system.

title: Effects outside, visibility inside
teaching: The host performs Git, filesystem, process, signer, and agent effects; projection turns canonical state into readable status without becoming another workflow engine.
question: Why should Mission Control display projections rather than calculate or mutate mission state itself?
whyItMatters: Keeping effects and presentation outside the pure kernel makes the system portable and testable.

title: Who decides, who acts, and when work stops
teaching: Seat contracts preserve specialized responsibility while green signals should move routine work automatically.
question: Which decisions remain human, which transitions should be automatic, and what conditions genuinely justify parking a team?
whyItMatters: This is the core balance between trustworthy governance and the speed you want from the team.

title: Track layers take trucks to work
teaching: The replacement rail is built in Track-Layer Mode under one bounded Epic Wheels Up decision; it is not forced to ride the defective system it replaces.
question: What does Epic Wheels Up authorize once, and what material changes would still require the team to return to you?
whyItMatters: This construction model is what converts a large architecture into autonomous progress without abandoning human control.

title: Issues as executable construction packets
teaching: Each issue must carry enough exact scope, dependencies, acceptance criteria, paths, and validation information for a team to act without rediscovering the architecture.
question: What must every issue packet contain so a fresh team can implement it without improvising hidden contracts?
whyItMatters: The issue graph is where architectural intent becomes repeatable team execution.

title: Portable execution and selective legacy extraction
teaching: Seat meaning remains stable across Factory, Codex, Copilot, and local models, while old code is harvested only when it fits the new boundary cleanly.
question: What should remain invariant across AI hosts, and what evidence should justify extracting old code instead of rebuilding it?
whyItMatters: This prevents both host lock-in and accidental reconstruction of the legacy ball of twine.

title: The order of construction
teaching: The flights build identity first, then the pure rail, storage and lanes, host composition, and finally the thin CLI and proving issue.
question: Does this sequence prove the riskiest assumptions early enough, and are any dependencies ordered incorrectly?
whyItMatters: A sound architecture can still fail if its implementation order creates unnecessary coupling or delays the first real proof.

title: The proof and your GO decision
teaching: The architecture succeeds only when a cold Hill carries one curated issue from intake through visible QA and draft PR while returning the lane to ready.
question: Would the first-flight evidence convince you Mission Rail is real, and what must change in this architecture before you give Epic Wheels Up?
whyItMatters: This checkpoint turns the document review into a concrete decision about starting the new rail.
